placements.originalParent: A **mass-spring system** is a mass hooked up to a spring, and it vibrates because of what each part wants. **The spring wants to be at its equilibrium position**, its resting length, so whenever it is stretched or squished it pulls or pushes to get back there. **A mass that is moving wants to keep on moving**, so once it gets going it does not stop on its own.
placements.text: Reaching **equilibrium** means the spring has reached its resting length. It does not mean the mass has stopped. The mass still has motion at that point, which is why returning toward equilibrium becomes an ongoing cycle rather than a single trip back.

placements.originalParent: Two things set how fast a mass-spring system vibrates, and they are the **mass** and the **stiffness** of the spring. The number of back-and-forth cycles the system completes each second is called its **frequency**.
placements.text: The prediction concerns **how quickly the cycle repeats**, rather than how far the mass travels. To explain a slower vibration, connect the added mass to the greater difficulty of reversing its motion while the spring stays the same.

placements.originalParent: With **two masses**, the system has two walls, a spring from each wall to a mass, and one spring between the two masses. All the masses are equal and all the springs are equal, and this system can vibrate in **two different ways**, which are called **modes**. **A mode is just another word for a way of vibrating**, and the two modes are told apart by asking whether the masses go together or against each other.
placements.text: **Mode 1 and mode 2 name patterns of the whole system.** They do not name the first and second masses. Both masses participate in either pattern, and the distinction is whether their movements agree or oppose one another.

placements.originalParent: With **three masses**, the system has **three modes**, one more than with two masses, and each mode is a different way the masses move relative to each other. In the first mode all three go back and forth together, and this mode has the lowest frequency. In the second mode the middle mass stays perfectly still while the two outer masses move against each other, and this is the middle frequency. In the third mode the middle mass moves opposite to the two outer masses, and this is the highest frequency.
placements.text: A still middle mass is part of the **second-mode pattern**. Its stillness does not turn the system into a two-mass system. The three masses still permit three modes, with the middle mass participating differently in each one.

placements.originalParent: The **spectrum** of a sound tells which frequencies are in it and how much of each there is.
placements.text: A spike’s **frequency** tells which vibration it represents, while its **amplitude** tells how much of that vibration is present. A taller spike means a stronger contribution, rather than a faster vibration.

placements.originalParent: For the voice, the theory says that **the vocal folds are a membrane** built from many masses and springs, so they vibrate in many modes at once. Their equations are the same type as the spring equations, only more of them and slightly more complicated, so the intuition built from masses and springs is enough to reason with. The prediction is that **any laryngeal vibration signal will have a spectrum with evenly spaced spikes**, and these evenly spaced spikes are called **harmonics**.
placements.text: The test is whether the measured spikes follow the predicted **regular spacing**. Different voices can begin at different frequencies and still support the same prediction, because each voice has its own lowest frequency and multiples of that frequency.

placements.originalParent: This changes which modes are possible, because **only the odd harmonics occur**, meaning one, three, five and seven times the lowest frequency. The modes at two and four times the lowest frequency are missing, because those patterns cannot end with free motion at the top.
placements.text: The **second mode** is the second allowed pattern. In this fixed–free system it is three times the lowest frequency, rather than twice that frequency. Counting allowed modes and counting multiples of the lowest frequency therefore give different numbers.

placements.originalParent: **Making the middle mass heavier** affects only the modes in which that mass moves.
placements.text: The physical change is the same heavier middle mass in every case. What differs is the **mode being considered**. One change can therefore lower the first and third mode frequencies while leaving the second unchanged.

placements.originalParent: **Where there is maximal movement there is no stretching, and where there is maximal stretching there is no movement.** So **increasing a spring's stiffness raises frequency in proportion to how much that spring stretches and compresses**, which also depends on where it is.
placements.text: A point can remain still while the material beside it stretches and compresses. **No local displacement does not mean no restoring action.** The stiffness effect depends on that changing separation between neighboring parts, rather than on how far the marked point travels.

placements.originalParent: On a string, one small section is marked where the **fourth mode is moving a lot** while the **fifth mode has no motion at all but lots of stretching**. Raising both the mass and the stiffness of that section has a different effect on each mode, so each effect has to be reasoned out separately.
placements.text: Both changes are made at **one marked location**. The opposite results come from the fourth and fifth modes using that location differently, rather than from moving the added mass to one spot and the added stiffness to another.

placements.originalParent: A **building** is a system fixed on one side and free on the other. Structural engineers design it to sway in the first mode, all together, and never in higher modes, where some floors would go one way while others go the other way. **The air inside the vocal tract is also fixed on one side and free on the other.**
placements.text: **Fixed and free describe the air’s motion at the two ends of the model.** The closed vocal-fold end prevents the adjacent air from moving back and forth, while the open lip end permits that motion. The analogy concerns those endpoint conditions.

placements.originalParent: The first two modes matter most for vowels. The first mode corresponds to **F1**, the lowest air mode of the tube, with its motion still at the glottis and growing toward the lips. The second mode corresponds to **F2**, and it vibrates three times faster than the first.
placements.text: Calling F2 the **second formant** puts it second in the ordering of the air resonances. It does not say that its frequency is twice F1. The three-times relationship belongs to the uniform fixed–free tube illustrated here.

placements.originalParent: In the uniform tube for **schwa** and in the separate rows for the first, second and third modes, some places have air **moving a lot** and others have air **compressing a lot**, and the two alternate along the tube. **Motion** is how far a bit of air travels back and forth, while **compression** is how much the spacing between neighboring bits of air changes.
placements.text: Follow the **spacing between adjacent lines of air** as well as their travel. Lines can move a long way together without being squeezed closer to each other. Compression is the change in their spacing, so large motion by itself does not establish large compression.

placements.originalParent: The first principle is the simplest one. **As mass goes up, frequency goes down, and as stiffness goes up, frequency goes up.** That principle by itself invites a **false argument**, because if something raises both the mass and the stiffness of a system, it can seem that the two effects cancel and nothing audible changes.
placements.text: Opposite tendencies alone do not establish cancellation. For a frequency to stay unchanged, the effective increases must actually balance. In a system with many parts, the **location of the change and the mode’s movement there** decide how strongly each tendency counts.

placements.originalParent: The basic piece from a node to an antinode is called a **quarter-wave packet**, and each mode of a system with one free end holds an odd number of them. The first mode holds one packet, the second holds three, the third holds five and the fourth holds seven.
placements.text: A **quarter-wave packet** is a piece of the spatial pattern. Adding more of those pieces within the same overall length produces a higher allowed frequency. The requirement to finish at a free, moving end is what excludes an even packet count.

placements.originalParent: The first mode corresponds to **F1**, the lowest air mode of the tube, with its motion still at the fixed end and growing toward the free end. The second mode corresponds to **F2**, and it fits three of the pieces that run from no motion to lots of motion, while the first mode fits only one.
placements.text: For example, if this uniform tube has F1 at **200 Hz**, its second and third formants are **600 Hz and 1,000 Hz**. The useful reasoning is one, three and five times the first frequency; 200 is an illustrative starting value rather than a value shared by every vocal tract.

placements.originalParent: **The first mode of the air is the same idea as a building swaying in its first mode.** There is no motion at the bottom but lots of compression and expansion there, and there is lots of motion at the top but no compression.
placements.text: The still locations belong to a particular **mode pattern**. They do not mean that all the air has stopped. Air elsewhere in that same mode continues to move, while neighboring regions compress and expand around the still locations.

placements.originalParent: **A recording confirms what the reasoning predicts.** Starting from schwa, a student moved into /u/, and both the first and second formants dropped.
placements.text: The comparison starts with **schwa and then changes to /u/** in the same voice. Both formants moving downward is the predicted result of loading the freely moving lip region, so the measurement checks the mechanism rather than just naming the vowel.

placements.originalParent: **A recording confirms this prediction as well.** Starting from schwa and moving into /i/, the first formant dropped a lot and the second formant went up.
placements.text: **F1 falling while F2 rises** is especially informative because the two changes go in opposite directions. The result follows from one constriction meeting a mass-dominated part of one mode and a stiffness-dominated part of the other.

placements.originalParent: The **filter** is the air in the vocal tract, and **the vocal tract filter sculpts the heights of those harmonics**. For schwa, the filter places its formants evenly up the spectrum.
placements.text: The filter acts on the **harmonics already supplied by the source**. A formant indicates where that source energy is favored. It does not replace the harmonic comb with a new set of spikes at the formant frequencies.

placements.originalParent: The air does **two different things** at different places, and both can be seen directly. Where the slivers of air come very close together and then move far apart, the air is compressing and expanding, which is **springiness**, and that happens near the closed end, because air can be squeezed against something closed. Where the slivers stay equally spaced and just move back and forth, the air is acting like a **mass**, and that happens near the open end, because there is nothing there to squeeze against.
placements.text: The visible evidence for springiness is that neighboring air slices **approach and separate**. When the slices travel together at nearly constant separation, their visible behavior instead emphasizes the moving mass. This distinction lets the animation support a causal explanation.

placements.originalParent: **F0 is not fixed during speech.** Only a robot keeps F0 constant, while real speech changes F0 all the time, in every vowel.
placements.text: The same words, **“the dog slept here,”** can become a statement or a question as their pitch contour changes. That change concerns the vocal-fold vibration and its F0, while the vowel’s formant pattern concerns the shape of the tract.

placements.originalParent: The formants interact with the harmonics by one **core rule**, which is that **a formant encourages the closest harmonics to be audible, while harmonics far from that formant are muted.** Harmonics near a formant get amplified, and harmonics farther away get weaker until they cannot be heard.
placements.text: The harmonic nearest a formant becomes prominent **at the harmonic’s own frequency**. The formant shapes the relative strengths of the available harmonics; it does not require a harmonic to sit exactly at the resonance.

placements.originalParent: Now picture very light, very stiff vocal folds, whose harmonics are widely spaced. The first formant may have no harmonic close by to amplify, so **sparse harmonics can miss a formant or make it look ambiguous**.
placements.text: A formant can still be a resonance even when **no harmonic lies close enough to show it clearly**. Sparse source harmonics make the filter harder to read from the resulting spectrum, which explains why a high-pitched voice can obscure the vowel pattern.

placements.originalParent: **A spectrum captures one instant, and a spectrogram stacks many spectra over time.** Time runs along the horizontal axis, frequency runs up the vertical axis, and darkness tells how much energy there is, with high amplitude black, medium gray and low white. So a formant appears as a dark band at its frequency, and its rise and fall over time can be followed.
placements.text: The amplitude shown by **height in a spectrum** becomes **darkness in a spectrogram**. Frequency still identifies which vibration is present, while the added time axis shows how those strengths and formant locations develop as the mouth moves.

placements.originalParent: **Listeners decide which consonant they heard mostly from the vowel that follows it.** In the a that follows m, the formants stay fairly stationary, while in the a that follows n, one formant drops sharply. That drop in a formant inside the vowel tells the listener n, so it overrides the m that was pasted in front.
placements.text: The crucial manipulation keeps the **consonant from ma** but supplies the **vowel from na**. Hearing na shows that the decision about the consonant uses the following vowel’s transition, rather than being fixed by the isolated consonant segment alone.

placements.originalParent: This network only multiplies and adds, with **no activation functions** between the layers. It takes two inputs, passes them through three hidden layers, and ends in five outputs, and the two inputs are F1 and F2, the frequencies of the first two modes of the air's vibration.
placements.text: One pair of formant measurements leads to **one decision across five alternatives**. The five output neurons represent competing vowel identities for that same input, rather than five different recordings.

placements.originalParent: **The weights are the network's knowledge.** Every connection between two neurons has a weight, a positive or negative number, and everything the network knows about vowels is stored in these numbers.
placements.text: The **formant values** describe the particular recording being recognized. The **weights** describe how the network uses those values. A new recording supplies new inputs, while learning changes the weights that will be used to process recordings.

placements.originalParent: After the last layer, the final numbers are turned into a **probability distribution**, which is a set of numbers that add up to one, and those numbers are the network's decision. The operation that does this is called **softmax**, and it just converts numbers into probabilities, so a bigger score always ends up as a bigger probability.
placements.text: Adding up to one makes the output a **valid probability distribution**, but it does not make the answer correct. The largest probability can still belong to the wrong vowel. Correctness requires comparing the prediction with the known vowel.

placements.originalParent: The output the network actually produced is called the **computed output**, and the gap between it and the desired output is the **error**. Here the network gave dean only a small chance when it should have given dean all of it, so the error is large. **Backpropagation** is the algorithm that changes all the weights so that the network becomes a little smarter.
placements.text: The **desired output** comes from knowing which vowel produced the recording. It supplies the standard against which the computed output is judged. Learning changes the network’s weights to approach that standard, rather than changing the answer to agree with the network.

placements.originalParent: **The weight from the last hidden layer to done is an easy problem.** Done's large probability comes from an inner product that includes this positive weight times a positive activation. If the weight went up, that contribution would grow, done's probability would go up, and the network would get more wrong, since done should have no probability at all.
placements.text: For this marked connection, a **positive activation and positive weight** contribute positively to done. Making that weight smaller reduces its contribution. The explanation depends on this connection’s sign and destination, rather than on a rule that every weight should decrease.

placements.originalParent: **Improving W2 is a much harder problem.** W2 affects its own activations, which then affect another two layers of activations along with many other weights, so it is really hard to figure out how much blame W2 deserves for mistakes made all the way at the end.
placements.text: The difficult early-weight problem **contains the downstream problem**. Solving from the output backward makes the downstream error information available when its contribution is needed for an earlier connection, instead of treating each early weight as an unrelated problem.

placements.originalParent: **When a problem contains smaller and smaller problems inside it, the algorithm to use is dynamic programming.** Dynamic programming solves the easiest problem first and then uses its answer to solve the next bigger one, and it comes from Bellman and Viterbi.
placements.text: **Dynamic programming supplies the order and reuse of the error calculation. SGD supplies the gradual adjustment of the weights.** Together they explain both why the calculation starts near the output and how repeated small changes improve the network.

placements.originalParent: To train the network, it has to be told **the desired output for every input**, and that information is given as **two matrices**, which are just tables of numbers. Both come from the class's own lab data, with one row for each recording.
placements.text: The zeros in a **one-hot target** do not stand for missing recordings. Each zero says that its vowel is not the answer for this row, while the single one identifies the vowel that actually produced this pair of formants.

placements.originalParent: **The word Sequential means that the network is a sequence of layers**, one layer after another, which describes every network built so far. **The word Linear means a layer that does inner products** by multiplying and adding.
placements.text: **Sequential specifies the order of the layers, and Linear specifies the weighted multiplication and addition within a processing layer.** Those lines describe how information will be processed. The learning commands are what use an error to improve the weights.

placements.originalParent: The last lines are the only lines PyTorch needs for learning. **SGD** is stochastic gradient descent with a learning rate that sets the size of each step, the **loss** is the mistake, the gap between the computed and desired outputs, **backward** is backpropagation, and **step** actually changes the weights.
placements.text: **Backward** works out how the error depends on the weights, and **step** applies the weight changes. The backward calculation is part of learning; an ordinary prediction still carries the input forward toward the output.

placements.text: The steep middle and flatter ends explain why sigmoid behaves **almost like a switch** while still allowing intermediate values. The output is bounded, but the curve remains gradual rather than assigning only an exact zero or an exact one.

placements.originalParent: The sigmoid is added **one hidden neuron at a time**, while the input and every weight stay the same. The first neuron to switch has an inner product just below zero, on the steep middle of the curve, so it comes out just under one half and now sends a positive number instead of a negative one.
placements.text: When one hidden activation changes, **every downstream layer must use that new value**. Keeping the connection weights unchanged does not keep later activations unchanged, because their inputs have just changed.

placements.originalParent: The command **nn.Sigmoid** is added after each of the first three linear layers, and it means apply the sigmoid, which makes the neurons digital. The layer sizes stay exactly the same, because the sigmoid changes the values but not how many there are.
placements.text: **Linear computes a weighted sum; Sigmoid transforms the result of that sum.** Placing Sigmoid after a hidden linear layer gives those two operations a definite order before the resulting activations enter the next layer.

placements.originalParent: **Accuracy starts at twenty percent because that is the level of chance.** At the start the weights are random, so the network knows nothing, but it still is not at zero, because with five vowels a random guess is right one time in five.
placements.text: **Knowing nothing does not imply zero correct guesses.** With five alternatives, a random guess can still land on the right vowel. The one-in-five chance level explains the approximate 20% starting accuracy before the weights carry useful knowledge.

placements.originalParent: The same training is run **ten times**, each time starting from different random weights, while everything else stays identical. All ten runs start near chance, some leave chance quickly and others stay flat longer, and several briefly drop back toward chance. After a few hundred epochs they come together, and **all ten finish at the same accuracy, a little below half**.
placements.text: The repeated runs keep the **same training data** and change the **starting weights**. Their different paths therefore show how the starting point affects learning, rather than comparing different sets of recorded vowels.

placements.originalParent: **The network levels off well below perfect accuracy because the data overlap so much.** Its final accuracy is clearly better than chance, so the network has learned something, but it is still pretty low, because AI is not magic.
placements.text: Similar final accuracy does not mean the runs took the same route. The important contrast is **different learning paths reaching a similar limit**, with the overlap in the two-formant data helping explain why that limit remains below perfect recognition.

placements.originalParent: **The network is called recurrent because it takes its output and sends it back into part of its input.** It produces something at one moment, that output loops back into the state units, and the network uses it to predict the next moment, and then the moment after that.
placements.text: This feedback carries information about **what the system just produced into its next moment of processing**. It is different from describing the backward error calculation used to learn the weights. The recurrence gives the running network a history.

placements.originalParent: **A large language model takes in many lists of numbers, one for each moment in a sequence, and gives back one decision about what comes next.** Here it takes fifteen vectors, each standing for something at one moment in time, such as one word of a sentence, and its job is to predict the sixteenth.
placements.text: The **number of vectors** tells how many items are in the context, while the **numbers within each vector** describe an item. These are two different dimensions of the representation, so a long context is not the same thing as a large vector.

placements.originalParent: **A large language model learns by predicting the next word and correcting its mistakes.** Given the cat sat on the, with mat as the real next word, a new model with random weights predicts something silly like in, and backpropagation adjusts all of its weights so that the prediction moves toward mat.
placements.text: A real sequence supplies the **training answer**. Hiding the next word in an existing sentence gives the model something to predict and then compare against, so the next-word task creates repeated opportunities to correct the weights.

placements.originalParent: **An agentic system is a graph of large language models**, and an agent in AI today is just one of these models. One model outlines the answer, another writes it out in smooth sentences, a **critic** criticizes the draft, a reviser sends it back to the critic if it is not good enough, and a final model produces the output.
placements.text: The outline, draft, criticism and revision are **different jobs assigned to whole language models**. Passing the draft back for another criticism forms a loop, so this example is organized by the roles and messages between models.

placements.originalParent: **A large language model takes fifteen vectors and predicts the sixteenth**, and since a vector is just a list of numbers, those numbers can stand for almost anything. Whatever they stand for, the machine plays the same game of predicting the next one.
placements.text: **Fifteen vectors and a sixteenth prediction are the small example.** The organizing idea is to use the available context to predict the next item. The same idea applies when the context contains many more items.

placements.originalParent: **Inference uses learned weights to process an input, while learning changes those weights.** Inner products supply the weighted combinations used in inference, and stochastic gradient descent adjusts the weights using the backward calculation organized through dynamic programming.
placements.text: During **inference**, the learned weights supply the knowledge used to produce a response. During **learning**, the mismatch with a known target is used to revise that knowledge. Producing a new response and improving the weights are different operations.

placements.originalParent: **Several heads work in parallel inside each layer.** Each acts as a different expert, contributing information that the layer combines with the contributions of the other heads. The result is a new set of representations that brings those contributions together.
placements.text: Calling a head an **expert** means that it has learned weights for contributing to the numerical representation. It is a component inside the language model, rather than a separate model that receives an outline or writes a draft.

placements.originalParent: **The following layer repeats the process using the representations it receives.** Its heads again work in parallel, and their contributions are combined before the vectors continue onward.
placements.text: The diagram has both **width and depth**. Several heads contribute within one layer, and successive layers transform the combined representations again. More heads and more layers therefore describe different aspects of the organization.

placements.originalParent: **An LLM develops its vectors through successive layers, so depth plays the role of time in this comparison.** One layer transforms the vectors, and the next layer uses those transformed vectors as its own input.
placements.text: The comparison follows the **representation as it develops through the model**. Each stage starts from what the preceding stage produced. This explains the dynamical-system connection without treating an LLM’s changing numerical trajectory as a literal spring oscillation.

placements.originalParent: **The vectors can represent pieces of sound or a picture.** A spectrogram is divided into consecutive frames, and the model predicts the next frame of sound. A picture is divided into patches read row by row, and the task is to predict the missing bottom-right patch.
placements.text: Sound already unfolds in time, while the picture is given an **order by its sequence of patches**. What the prediction task needs in both cases is a sequence of vector representations and a next item to predict.

placements.originalParent: **Guessing the next letter is the same as predicting the sixteenth item**, which is the same game of predicting the next token that a large language model plays. A GPT trained only on this game learns English sounds and spelling, because its predictions can only get good by matching the patterns of English syllables.
placements.text: **Good next-letter predictions require knowledge of the patterns in the words.** Repeated prediction and correction can put those constraints into the weights, even though the immediate task is to guess a continuation rather than recite a list of phonotactic rules.
